Krichene and Rendle show that sampled ranking metrics can reverse model ordering relative to full-catalog evaluation, even in expectation. Smaller candidate sets distort top-heavy metrics; very small samples make metrics behave increasingly like AUC. Fixed negatives improve reproducibility but do not remove this bias. Thus HR@10 against 99 negatives measures performance within that sampled benchmark, not full-catalog HR@10. Proposed statistical corrections introduce bias–variance tradeoffs and should not replace the pinned host metric. [On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

Practical implication for this task: preserve the host’s 200 validation users/category, 99 unique negatives, evaluation seed 42, and macro-average HR@10 across all four categories. For paired model or history-perturbation comparisons, reuse identical users, targets, candidate identities and candidate order; compare per-user hit differences before aggregation. Document the host’s exact seen-item exclusion, repeated-target eligibility and score-tie rules, including whether a held-out target previously observed in history remains eligible. Do not silently deduplicate histories, remove repeated targets, resample candidates after perturbation, or substitute a different tie-breaking convention. These are reproducibility recommendations inferred from the evaluation problem, rather than guarantees established by the paper. Keep the simulator’s full-catalog unseen-item recommendations separate from sampled validation; neither score should be interpreted as the other.
